nameStory: This moth earned its "horned" name from the distinctive horn-like projections that stick out from its wings, giving it an almost otherworldly appearance. The "spanworm" part comes from its caterpillar stage, which moves by arching its body like it's measuring or "spanning" distances with each step. It's also called the "filament bearer" because of the delicate, thread-like extensions on its wings.
description: The Horned Spanworm Moth is a small, delicate member of the geometer moth family with one of the most unusual wing shapes you'll see on any moth. Its wingspan measures less than an inch across (about 19-25mm), but what it lacks in size it makes up for in distinctive appearance. The wings have dramatic pointed projections that extend outward like tiny horns or spikes, creating an unmistakable silhouette. These pale, earth-toned moths are active from late spring through summer in New England.

idTips.label: Wing projections
idTips.description: Look for the dramatic pointed spikes or "horns" extending from the wings - no other small moth in New England has these distinctive thread-like projections that make the moth look almost star-shaped when spread out

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: A small, delicate moth with a wingspan smaller than a quarter, with a slender body and relatively broad wings for its size

idTips.label: Wing color
idTips.description: Pale brownish or grayish wings with subtle darker markings and a somewhat translucent quality that gives them a papery feel if handled gently

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat weak, fluttering motion and is easily attracted to porch lights and windows on warm evenings

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings horizontally outward from the body, making the horn-like projections very obvious and creating a distinctive cross-like silhouette

habitat: Found throughout New England's mixed forests, suburban areas, and anywhere their host plants grow. You'll encounter them around both coniferous trees like hemlocks, firs, and spruces, as well as deciduous trees including birches, willows, and hazels. They're equally at home in deep woods and backyard gardens, often showing up at porch lights in residential areas near these trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May in northern New England, earlier in southern areas. Look for them at porch lights and windows during warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time when adults are most commonly seen, especially June through August. This is your best chance to spot them attracted to lights at night.
seasonality.fall: In southern New England, a second generation may appear in early fall, though numbers are typically lower than the summer peak.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they overwinter as pupae in the soil or leaf litter, waiting for spring warmth to trigger emergence.

funFact: Despite being called spanworms, the caterpillars of this species are incredibly versatile eaters - they can munch on everything from towering spruce trees to tiny wild strawberry plants, and even carrot tops in your garden, making them one of the least picky eaters in the moth world!
confusionNotes: The wing projections make this moth nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England - no other small moth has these dramatic spiky extensions. If you see horn-like projections on the wings, you've found your horned spanworm moth!
contextualKnowledge: This species was originally lumped together with a European moth but was recognized as a separate North American species in 1856. The scientific name "resistaria" roughly means "standing firm" or "resistant," though the reason for this name choice by the original describer remains a mystery.
compareHints: This is the only Nematocampa species in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Among other geometer moths, it's instantly distinguishable by its wing projections - most other geometers have simple triangular or rounded wing shapes. The closest you might find are some of the larger prominent moths, but those are much bigger and lack the delicate, thread-like wing extensions.
